question: What is a token?
answers: One complete sentence of the prompt text
A chunk of text, often part of a word
One paid question to the model
A single letter, digit or symbol
fact: Models read and write in small chunks of text called tokens, usually a short word or part of one. Your prompt, documents and the answer are all counted in them.

question: Roughly how many English words are in 1,000 tokens?
fact: A handy rule: one token is about four characters, or three quarters of a word. So 1,000 tokens is roughly 750 words of English.

question: A CFO asks which usually costs more per token in the API. Best answer?
answers: Output tokens, what the model writes
Neither: only the seat is billed
fact: Writing is the model's slow, step-by-step work, so output tokens usually cost several times more than input. Long reports cost more than short classifications.

question: What does the context window measure?
answers: How many users it can serve at once
How long the vendor keeps all your chats
How much text it can consider at once
fact: Think of it as the model's working desk, measured in tokens. Once the desk is full, something has to come off.

question: A customer asks why providers offer small and large model tiers. Best answer?
answers: To separate free users from paying ones
To match model size to task difficulty
To store more data in each chat
fact: Big models are smartest and priciest; small ones are fast and cheap. Simple jobs like sorting or extracting rarely need the biggest one.

question: When does latency matter most?
fact: Latency is how long you wait. A customer on a live call needs speed; an overnight job does not. Ask which kind of workload it is before recommending a model.

question: Per-seat pricing keeps everyday staff chat more predictable than per-token pricing.
fact: Seats are a flat cost per person, so the bill stays predictable however much people use it.

question: What do input tokens cover in a long chat?
answers: The words the model writes back
The system prompt and nothing else
fact: Everything you send counts as input: instructions, the conversation so far, and any documents. The answer the model writes is counted separately, as output.

question: A finance lead asks why set spend limits and usage dashboards. Best answer?
answers: To make the model answer more quickly
So finance isn't surprised by usage
fact: Token bills scale with use, so alerts and caps prevent nasty surprises and show which workloads are growing.

question: Illustrative prices: $2 per million tokens in, $8 out. Cost of 2M in, 1M out?
fact: These prices are made up for illustration; always check the current pricing page. 2M input is $4, 1M output is $8, so $12 in total.

question: A support bot handles 10,000 chats a day at 3,000 input tokens each. Input tokens a day?
fact: 10,000 chats times 3,000 tokens gives 30 million. Do the maths aloud with round, illustrative prices, then compare with the human work the bot supports.

question: A customer works in Thai and Bahasa. How should costs be estimated?
answers: Test on their real local text
Assume the same ratio as English
fact: Other languages can split into more tokens for the same meaning. Test cost on real data instead of assuming English ratios.

question: Which choice usually saves the most money first?
answers: Always use the biggest reasoning setting
Include the full archive in each prompt
Right-size the model to each task
Ask for longer, more detailed answers
fact: Small cheap models handle routing and classification well, and large ones are kept for hard reasoning. Routing between them often cuts the bill sharply.

question: A long set of rules starts every request. Which saving applies?
answers: Batch processing for all the live chats
Prompt caching on the repeated part
fact: When every request begins with the same content, the provider can reuse that work. Repeated content gets cheaper and replies start sooner.

question: A customer processes thousands of documents overnight. What saves cost?
answers: The Batch API at a discount
fact: If nobody is waiting for the answer, you can trade speed for a lower price. Non-urgent jobs are exactly what the Batch API is for.

question: A reasoning model's hidden thinking is billed as tokens too.
fact: The thinking happens as tokens, and they are billed even though you do not see them. More reasoning effort means more waiting and a bigger bill, so use it where it earns its keep.

question: How should a customer choose between model tiers?
answers: Always begin with the top tier
Pick the tier with the longest window
Start cheapest and test on their eval
fact: Run the same eval set on the cheaper tier first. If it passes, you save money; move up only when the results show you need to.

question: Replies run to a page when users need two lines. Which lever fits best?
fact: Output tokens usually cost the most per token. Capping length and asking for brevity trims them directly, while caching only helps repeated input.

question: Which workload suits per-token API pricing best?
answers: Staff drafting emails in a chat app
fact: A product that serves many customers scales with usage, so paying per token tracks the value it brings.

question: What is the right ROI start for a CFO?
answers: Count how many prompts were written
Compare seat cost with last year's
Baseline two or three workflows first
fact: Pick specific workflows, measure time, volume and errors today, pilot, then compare. Use the customer's own numbers, never a generic percentage.

question: A customer fears 'token burn'. Where does spend usually come from?
answers: A few oversized or bloated workloads
Every employee using the tool equally
The cost of storing old chat history
Fixed monthly licence fees on seats
fact: Look before you cut. Spend is usually concentrated in a few workloads with an oversized model or too much context, and right-sizing and trimming often fix most of it.

question: Illustrative: $2/M in, $8/M out. 1,000 calls of 2,000 in, 500 out cost?
fact: Input is 2M tokens, so $4. Output is 0.5M tokens, so $4. Total $8. Say the prices are illustrative, then compare with the cost of the human work.

question: An ROI sum uses a 'loaded' hourly cost. What does loaded mean?
answers: The top salary in the team
Salary plus the AI tool's cost
fact: A loaded cost counts the full cost of an hour of someone's time: pay, benefits and overheads. It makes time-saved sums realistic. Use the customer's figures, not a guess.

question: A customer wants to self-host to avoid token fees. A fair pitch?
answers: Hybrid: open weights for simple volume
Stay on the largest model for all work
Wait until token prices fall further
fact: Be honest about the trade-off. Open weights can suit high-volume simple work while frontier models handle the hard tasks. Then build a total cost comparison together.

question: A live voice agent feels slow. Which change helps most?
answers: Switch to the Batch API for lower cost
Use a larger window for more memory
Add a longer system prompt of rules
fact: Live conversations are latency-sensitive. A smaller model and less thinking per turn cut the wait, while batch processing and bigger windows do nothing for speed.

question: Which number best shows a seat rollout is working?
answers: The size of the vendor invoice
How long the logo stays on screen
fact: Bought seats are not used seats. Weekly active users, and the share of seats in use, show real adoption and predict a healthy renewal.

question: Capping output length is one way to control cost.
fact: Output tokens usually cost more than input, so a sensible length cap and a clear brief about answer style keep bills down.

question: What does 'reasoning effort' control?
answers: How many users can log in
How long the context window is
How strict the safety rules are
How hard the model thinks first
fact: Higher effort means more hidden thinking, more tokens and more waiting. Use low for simple tasks and high for hard ones.

question: To forecast an API bill, which two numbers matter most?
answers: Seats bought and logins per week
Calls per day and tokens per call
fact: Cost is roughly calls times tokens per call times price. Estimate calls per day and input and output tokens per call, then test with real samples.

question: Illustrative $1 per million input tokens. A 20,000-token file sent 1,000 times costs?
fact: 20,000 x 1,000 = 20 million tokens, which is 20 x $1 = $20. These are round, illustrative numbers, not a quote.

question: 200 staff each save 2 hours a week at an illustrative $30 an hour. Weekly value?
fact: 200 x 2 x $30 = $12,000. These numbers are illustrative; in practice use the customer's real loaded costs and a measured baseline.

question: A pilot's token bill is triple the forecast. What do you check first?
fact: Surprise bills usually trace to a few bloated prompts, loops that retry, or a bigger model than the task needs. Look at usage by workload before changing the plan.

question: A job reads long files and returns a one-word label. Cost profile?
answers: Mostly input tokens, with tiny output
Mostly output tokens, with tiny input
Costs the same on both sides
No cost, since labels are free
fact: Output tokens usually cost more, but here there are very few. Classification over long documents is typically cheap, and a smaller model often does it well.

question: A nightly job re-sends a 50-page guide with every row. What saves most?
answers: Shorten each answer to one word
Cache the guide and batch the rows
Move the guide to the output side
fact: Caching makes repeated prompt content cheaper, and the Batch API discounts work that is not urgent. Together they suit overnight jobs well.

question: A self-hosting quote lists only GPU hire. What's missing?
answers: Nothing: GPUs are the whole cost
A licence fee for every token
The team to run and monitor it
A separate fee for context windows
fact: Idle GPUs still cost money and a team must run, secure and update the stack. That staffing is often the biggest line, so compare total cost of ownership, not hardware alone.

question: Illustrative price: $1 per million tokens. What do 5 million tokens cost?
fact: Cost is tokens divided by a million, times the price. Five million tokens at $1 per million is $5. Real prices vary by model.

question: Roughly how many tokens is a 3,000-word English report?
fact: English runs at about three words for every four tokens, so 3,000 words is nearly 4,000 tokens.

question: Which is the usual first step for a bloated prompt?
fact: You pay for every input token on every call. Cutting repeated text lowers cost and often helps focus.

question: Images sent to a model are free of token charges.
fact: Images are converted to tokens and billed as input, with larger or more detailed images costing more. Test cost on the customer's real files.

question: A product serves millions of app users. Which pricing fits best?
answers: Per seat, one for each customer
A flat fee with no limits
fact: App usage grows and shrinks, and users are not staff. Usage-based pricing matches cost to actual traffic.

question: What is latency?
fact: Latency is the delay you feel. It matters in live chat and voice, less in overnight jobs.

question: Illustrative $3 per million output tokens. 400 replies of 500 tokens cost?
fact: 400 times 500 is 200,000 tokens, or 0.2 of a million. At $3 per million that is $0.60.

question: Illustrative $1/M in, $4/M out. One call: 10,000 in, 1,000 out. Cost?
fact: Input is 0.01 million at $1, so $0.01. Output is 0.001 million at $4, so $0.004. Together $0.014.

question: Bills are high because chats have very long histories. Which lever fits?
answers: Raise the cap on output length
fact: The whole history is resent each turn, so trimming or summarising it cuts input tokens on every later message.

question: A pilot works in testing but gets 'too many requests' errors at peak. Likely cause?
answers: A rate limit on requests or tokens
fact: Providers cap requests and tokens per minute, and going over returns an error. Plan capacity, add retries and ask about higher limits before launch.

question: Thai text carries the same meaning as English. What is the usual cost effect?
answers: Priced by words, so no difference
Often more: test on real text
fact: Tokenisers tuned mostly on English may split other scripts into more pieces, so cost and context use can rise. It varies by model.

question: When does self-hosting start to make cost sense?
answers: When the team simply prefers it
fact: Owned hardware is paid for whether it is busy or idle. It pays back only when kept well used.

question: A heavy daily user group wants predictable bills. Best fit?
answers: Pay per token with no cap
fact: Seats give a flat monthly cost per person, which finance can plan. Token billing rises with use.

question: A bot deflects 2,000 tickets a month, worth an illustrative $5 each, and costs $3,000 to run. Net gain?
fact: 2,000 times $5 is $10,000 of value. Take away the $3,000 running cost and $7,000 remains each month.

question: The reply looks short but the bill is large. Likely hidden cost?
fact: Reasoning models think before replying, and that hidden thinking is usually billed. Lower the effort setting for simple jobs.

question: Which figure tells a CFO more about value?
fact: Cost per task links spend to a business result, like a resolved ticket. Per-token prices alone say little about value.

question: Illustrative input prices: small $0.5/M, large $5/M. 80% of traffic is easy and goes small. Saving vs all-large?
fact: Blended price is 0.8 times 0.5 plus 0.2 times 5, so $1.40 against $5. That is roughly 70% lower.

question: Illustrative: a $2,000 daily bill, 60% batchable, with a 50% batch discount. Daily saving?
fact: 60% of $2,000 is $1,200 that can be batched. Half price on that saves $600 a day.

question: A pilot with 50 users costs $1,000 a month. Roll out to 5,000 at the same use. Rough estimate?
answers: Unchanged, as it is a fixed fee
fact: Usage-based cost scales roughly with users times use. 100 times the users is about 100 times the bill, so forecast before launch.

question: Prompt caching only helps when which is true?
answers: Whole answers repeat word for word
fact: Caching stores the repeated start of a prompt, so only the new part is processed. Prompts that differ from the start gain little.
